Turso / libSQL: concurrency & embedded replicas (MQLITE-4)

This guide follows main, including unreleased driver hardening. For an installed v0.4.2 release, use the Turso guide at that tag; see CHANGELOG.md for pending behavior changes.

MQLite runs the same engine on a local SQLite file or a remote Turso/libSQL database — set MQLITE_DB=libsql://<db>.turso.io (+ MQLITE_DB_AUTH_TOKEN). The remote path is CGO-free: it speaks Hrana over HTTP via libsql-client-go, so the single static binary still has no native deps. This note records how concurrency is handled and why embedded replicas are not used.

Rust-based Turso technical preview

Unreleased main also accepts turso://<database>.turso.io for a Rust-based Turso database. Supply its token through MQLITE_DB_AUTH_TOKEN or WithDBAuthToken, just as for a libsql:// database. MQLite uses the service's HTTP v2 compatibility endpoint with its existing pure-Go driver and connection-validity adapter; it normalizes the scheme inside the driver connection string. No native library or higher Go source floor is required.

The Rust service is a technical preview. Validate its queue operations, repeated opens, recovery and query performance with your workload before adopting it. MQLite still uses ordinary BEGIN transactions and requires one broker / Engine per database. A provider's concurrent-write capability does not enable BEGIN CONCURRENT or make multiple MQLite owners safe. The new provider's SQL compatibility and optimizer are independent of libSQL's; do not assume identical throughput or query plans.

Backend parity contract

Storage selection is a deployment detail, not a second API mode. Given the same committed state, broker time and request, local SQLite and remote Turso/libSQL MUST produce the same successful result, validation outcome, message/resource state transition and logical sentinel error. The HTTP status/code mapping and Go SDK errors.Is behavior therefore do not change when an operator changes the broker's database DSN. In particular, scheduling, delivery counts, settlement, ordering, deduplication, topic fan-out, deletion and TTL use one engine contract.

This is parity of deterministic queue behavior, not a claim that a local file and a network service have identical failure or performance envelopes. The documented differences are operational or failure-boundary concerns:

  • latency, throughput and temporary availability caused by the remote round trip;
  • remote transport/storage failures, including ErrOutcomeUnknown when a write may have committed but its acknowledgement was lost;
  • retry and cancellation mechanics during a storage fault — notably, a remote transactional-outbox callback may run more than once and must keep its effects transaction-bound;
  • deployment and maintenance controls: the local file lock, SQLite synchronous mode, file-size accounting and compaction have no identical remote operation; Turso still requires one logical MQLite owner but cannot use that local OS lock; and
  • explicitly operational observation fields such as backend identity and connection-pool data.

Those differences MUST NOT silently change a successful operation's queue semantics or turn a documented logical error into a backend-specific one. The hermetic suite locks the shared engine and error mappings on every PR; the credentials-gated nightly suite compares representative lifecycle, concurrency, settlement, access-key and TTL contracts with a real Turso database.

Concurrency model

MQLite has a single logical owner in both modes: each database has exactly one active MQLite broker or embedded Engine. Replace that owner stop-then-start after confirming the old process has exited. Do not use rolling overlap against the same database. What differs between storage modes is the connection pool:

local file / :memory: libsql:// / turso:// (HTTP Hrana) ws:// / wss://
write ownership 1 connection = local writer (file lock, MQLITE-6) one owner admits one write attempt at a time same remote ownership
provider pool MaxOpen=1, MaxIdle=1 MaxOpen=4, MaxIdle=0 MaxOpen=4, MaxIdle=2
observation file: 1 read-only connection; :memory:: writer connection provider-backed pool provider-backed pool
lifecycle ConnMaxLifetime=0 one logical Hrana connection per database/sql lease IdleTime=3s, Lifetime=55s
physical reuse SQLite connection stays open http.DefaultTransport still reuses TCP/TLS connections the WebSocket itself is pooled

Remote mutations wait for one cancellable write permit before acquiring a SQL connection. The permit covers one attempt through commit or rollback; retry backoff releases it. Renewals precede settlements in separate FIFO queues, with bounded bursts at each level so ordinary writes and maintenance also progress. Reads retain access to the four-connection pool. This cannot interrupt an already running transaction and does not make overlapping brokers or Engine instances safe.

A public Tx callback holds the write permit until that attempt finishes. Keep callbacks short and use the supplied EngineTx for business SQL and enqueueing. Complete the callback before waiting for another mutation through the same owner.

For HTTP Hrana, a direct queue batch transports bounded groups of parameterized statements together while retaining one transaction and one commit for the whole Send. Fan-out and expiring subscriptions retain their existing fenced paths. Network latency still contributes to transaction and lease budgets.

On libsql://, a lease is one ordinary operation or one complete transaction. Returning the lease discards its logical Hrana connection before it can enter an idle slot or be handed directly to a waiting caller; this does not tear down the shared HTTP transport or its TCP/TLS keep-alive connections. Each broker process shares its expensive all-queue observation query for about 10 seconds on both local and remote backends; separate brokers do not share that cache. Per-queue Stats and each observation's lightweight storage probe still use the backend shown above.

Connection resilience (the remote hardening)

An HTTP Hrana response can succeed with a null baton, which means the server has closed that logical stream. The pinned libsql-client-go records the closed state but does not implement driver.Validator. Without the MQLite adapter, database/sql can therefore put a known-closed connection in an idle slot or hand it directly to a waiting caller; the next operation then fails locally with a wrapped driver.ErrBadConn ("stream is closed: driver: bad connection") before making an HTTP request. An explicit *sql.Conn also cannot exchange its pinned driver connection underneath the caller.

MQLite prevents that stale handoff for libsql://: its compatibility adapter marks every logical connection invalid when the database/sql lease ends. A transaction remains one uninterrupted lease through commit or rollback. This is a connection-validity rule, not broader retry, caching or singleflight; physical HTTP/TLS reuse remains owned by Go's shared transport. Normal failure handling is still bounded as follows:

  • Bounded retry on transient errors only — maxConnAttempts = 6.
  • Reads retry on transport drops and definite remote aborts. retryable = remote && (isConnErr || isBusyErr || isExpiredRemoteTransactionErr) gates query/queryRowScan: a read is idempotent, so replaying it on a fresh pooled connection is always safe. isConnErr spans the whole transport-failure family — driver.ErrBadConn, a closed Hrana stream, and their siblings EOF / broken pipe / i/o timeout (behind a proxy like Fly a dropped connection reads as EOF, not RST). A single provider HTTP error leaf with status 408, 429, 499 or 5xx also follows this policy. Before COMMIT is attempted, inTx discards the failed transaction and may reopen the entire callback under the same six-attempt bound. A numeric provider status takes precedence over SQLite words in its response body.
  • Writes and COMMIT retry only after a proven rejection. Only a genuine before-dispatch driver.ErrBadConn or typed SQLITE_BUSY evidence permits transparent replay. Plain text such as database is locked, the Rust preview's exact Tursodb error: Database is busy, or an idle-transaction rollback message does not prove that an issued write or COMMIT was rejected. The pinned driver can discard a non-200 HTTP status and return exactly the same text as a normal SQL rejection. Those issued-write outcomes are ErrOutcomeUnknown, preserving the cause, instead of automatically repeating a possibly committed effect. Before COMMIT starts, a callback error can still discard and retry the entire transaction within the six-attempt budget. Local SQLite remains unchanged. Supported callbacks use EngineTx.SQL() only for business statements; they must not call its Commit/Rollback methods or issue transaction-control SQL. Engine owns those boundaries. Early caller commits bypass this stage contract.
  • Idle-transaction expiry is stage-sensitive. The exact provider explanation that an interactive transaction was rolled back because its stream was idle identifies the known expiry condition for reads and pre-COMMIT callback retries. These paths reopen the whole transaction, rebuilding time-sensitive arguments. Exhaustion keeps the existing connection counter category and optional transaction_expired detail. The same untyped text received after an issued standalone write or COMMIT stays outcome-unknown; the driver no longer exposes enough protocol information to prove its origin. Generic timeout/rollback text, joined causes and checkpoint failures do not authorize extra retries.
  • A lost write acknowledgement is outcome-unknown, not retried (MQLITE-59). Any other transport drop on a write/commit — the primary may have durably committed before the ack was lost — surfaces as ErrOutcomeUnknown (HTTP 503 outcome_unknown) instead of being blindly replayed into a double-insert. The caller reconciles by message_id/dedup before retrying; transparent recovery would need durable per-op idempotency, which is deferred. errors.Is(err, mqlite.ErrOutcomeUnknown) works in both embedded and client mode. Transient provider HTTP responses on an issued standalone write or COMMIT are also outcome-unknown: a proxy 502 does not prove that the primary rejected the effect. They are never automatically replayed; the error preserves its provider cause and HTTPStatus() for reconciliation and diagnostics. HTTP authentication and other nontransient responses are returned without blind retries. Provider HTTP failures keep the existing connection storage-counter category; optional details carry the safe status and provider_unavailable description, with outcome_unknown remaining authoritative for ambiguous writes. When fallback decoding discards the HTTP status, diagnostics do not invent it. Coded fallback errors cannot promote a remote write into a safe ErrBadConn retry. Supported remote mutations hold an explicit connection or transaction; MQLite does not issue standalone writes through sql.DB.ExecContext.
  • Never retry a logical storage error. A constraint violation or no such table is final inside the engine. At the HTTP client boundary, lifecycle deletion is more conservative: every HTTP 5xx is ErrOutcomeUnknown, because a gateway can synthesize that response after the broker committed and its acknowledgement was lost. Local stores never retry at all (a single conn is the single writer).

Transport caveat. The outcome-unknown guarantee holds for the documented remote transport libsql:// (Hrana-over-HTTP). The ws:///wss:// transports can wrap a response-read failure as ErrBadConn, under which a lost commit ack would be replayed — prefer libsql:// for at-least-once remote writes.

The null-baton, idle-pool, direct-waiter, authentication and transaction-lease contracts are tested hermetically by TestHranaClosedStreamIsDiscardedBeforeFreshReuse and TestHranaTransactionKeepsOneLease. The classifier is pinned by TestIsConnErr / TestRetryableWrite / TestRetryableAndAttempts in engine/storage_test.go, and broker→SDK propagation by TestFailOutcomeUnknown (server) + TestRemoteOutcomeUnknownPropagates (root), so the retry contract can't silently drift without credentials.

Ordinary and AttemptID Receive transactions issue their fenced UPDATE messages ... RETURNING before reading queue or receive-attempt metadata. This avoids upgrading a deferred read snapshot after another pooled connection has committed a write. The first update also verifies the queue lifecycle, absolute subscription expiry and claim-relevant cached configuration. If it returns no row, the same write transaction reads current metadata to distinguish an empty queue, deletion/expiry, stale configuration and an AttemptID replay. Batch continuation then uses the smaller indexed claim statement.

This write-first shape addresses claim transactions in one broker or embedded Engine. Remote retries remain bounded, other operations may still surface SQLITE_BUSY, and the change does not make overlapping brokers against one database safe.

Embedded replicas — evaluated, not adopted

Turso embedded replicas keep a local libSQL file that syncs from the remote primary: reads hit the local copy, writes go to the primary and sync back. They are a big win for read-heavy, geo-distributed read workloads. They are the wrong fit for MQLite, for two independent reasons:

  1. Async sync breaks queue consistency. A queue's reads (claim, peek) run against the same rows it just wrote and need read-after-write consistency: a claim must see its own state change atomically. A replica that lags the primary by even a sync interval could re-hand-out an already-claimed message or hide a just-enqueued one — exactly the correctness the Peek-Lock model exists to prevent. The broker is the single logical owner, so it gains nothing from a read replica of its own writes.
  2. They require CGO. Embedded replicas live in the native go-libsql binding, not the pure-Go libsql-client-go Hrana client MQLite uses. Adopting them would reintroduce CGO and cross-compilation pain — abandoning the CGO-free, single-static-binary goal that defines this project.

For HA / geo-distribution: co-locate the broker next to its Turso primary (low-latency Hrana), or run independent broker + DB pairs per region. Revisit this decision only when a maintained pure-Go driver satisfies synchronous read-your-writes semantics, the Go 1.21 floor and every supported release target.

Validation status

Functional checks exercised MQLite's queue and message contracts against standard Turso and the Rust-backed technical preview over libSQL-compatible HTTP/Hrana, using the unreleased compatibility candidate.

  • Transport: MQLite uses the pure-Go github.com/tursodatabase/libsql-client-go driver, pinned at v0.0.0-20251219100830-236aa1ff8acc. MQLite retains its Go 1.21 source floor. Rust preview checks used an unreleased URI adapter that maps turso:// to the same HTTP/Hrana transport. For v0.4.2, use the documented libsql:// URI.
  • Ownership and transactions: run one active broker or embedded Engine per database. MQLite uses ordinary transactions rather than BEGIN CONCURRENT; provider concurrent-write features do not change this ownership model.
  • Write acknowledgements: a lost COMMIT acknowledgement returns ErrOutcomeUnknown. Reconcile the operation before retrying; a disconnected response does not establish whether the write committed.
  • Deployment: place the broker near its Turso primary. Measure latency and throughput with your payloads, concurrency and batch sizes, then choose lease durations and request deadlines for that workload.

Repeatable test suites

Online compatibility statements refer to completed live checks against the stated backend and source candidate.

Run the live suite only against a dedicated, disposable test database. TestMain drops every MQLite-managed table before the selected tests begin, including when -run selects one test, so the reset requires an explicit confirmation:

MQLITE_TEST_DB=libsql://<db>.turso.io MQLITE_TEST_DB_AUTH_TOKEN=<jwt> \
  MQLITE_TEST_DB_RESET_CONFIRM=1 \
  go test ./engine -run TestTurso -v

Without MQLITE_TEST_DB the live tests skip; the hermetic classifier test always runs.
